newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Wide support for Zaire opposition strike.
newsitem.headline: Wide support for Zaire opposition strike.

text.p: An opposition strike call closed down much of Zaire's capital Kinshasa on Monday, drawing far wider support than the last such protest in 1995.
The main opposition Sacred Union of the Radical Opposition (USOR) of Etienne Tshisekedi called the protest to demand the removal of Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo.

The opposition, which has called for negotiations with rebels in the east who have captured a strip of territory, attacked Kengo's conduct towards the war and accused him of stalling on promised elections.
"It's a total success. The dead town (protest) has been following throughout the country," said Joseph Olenghankoy, leader of Tshisekedi's followers in the transitional parliament.
"Kengo must understand that the people no longer want him. He must go," Olenghankoy told Reuters.

Soldiers in military vehicles patrolled potential flashpoints and civil guards deployed at petrol stations that mostly stayed shut. In the Lemba residential district youths set fire to tyres but there were no immediate reports of violence.
Torrential rains fell on the sprawling city part way through the day -- offering an added incentive for people to stay home.
A similar protest called by the radical opposition in 1995 flopped with businesses and government offices working normally.

This time many private and public sector workers followed the call. The central bank and prime minister's offices operated but Kinshasa's business district -- where June 30 Boulevard is usually blocked by traffic jams -- was almost deserted.
Elsewhere, no newspapers appeared. Most taxi and mini-buses drivers followed the call. The usually bustling central market stayed shut but groups of vendors set out wares on its fringes.
Support for the strike in Kinshasa was not total.
"There's nothing special to report... It was business as usual at the prime minister's offices," a Kengo advisor said.
"I live from day to day. If I don't work my children don't eat," taxi driver Joseph Kabwe commented. "The politicians have tonnes of (food) stocks at home. I cannot follow their call."
There were no independent confirmation of the response elsewhere in the large Central African nation.

Rebel forces on Monday kept up their push towards a heavily fortified eastern airport and army base at Kindu. Kindu, a mining town, also has a large French-built airport and is 340 km (200 miles) west of the lakeside rebel-held town of Bukavu on the border with Rwanda.

A senior defence ministry official acknowledged that the government counter-offensive, launched on January 20, had failed to make major advances. He said the army planned to use planes and helicopter gunships to turn the tide against the rebels.
"The army will rely heavily on air strikes to defeat the rebels," he told Reuters on Sunday. "The counter-offensive has been launched but it has not got into high gear."
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila said in his headquarters on Sunday that his forces would target Kisangani, Zaire's third largest city and headquarters for the counter-offensive.
He said that the Tutsi-led rebels would not march on the village of Tingi Tingi where up to 130,000 frightened Rwandan Hutus have taken refuge, 200 km (125 miles) south of Kisangani.
U.N. refugee supremo Sadako Ogata, who visited the camp on Saturday, welcomed the decision. She was speaking in Kenya.

Ogata has expressed concern that rebel advances will further endanger up to 300,000 trapped Hutu refugees who fled Rwanda fearing reprisals after the 1994 genocide of minority Tutsis by hardline Hutus.
